## Setting
Reorganizing the neighbourhood refuse point. The collection point that five neighbouring households share has become a recurring source of complaints. The five representatives are settling on one arrangement with the ward office. Participants: Kenji, Servas, Mizuki, May and Midori. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- Ward subsidy and last year's shelter costs
- Block ledger of refuse-point expenses
- Ward filing requirements per the installations clerk
- Supervised mornings on the next lane
- Visit to the station block's bin house
- Truck arrival time from the crew leader
- Ward complaint log for this point
- Measurements of the five frontages
- The station block's meeting minutes
- Statements at the residents' meeting

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: May, Mizuki, Kenji, Midori and Servas. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the options | 4 turns | every participant votes; the option with the most votes is adopted |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied options is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Your profile
Name: Kenji
Age: 12
Gender: male
Personality: Kenji is curious and actively takes on challenges. He values his friends and enjoys communicating with those around him. Although he can be a little clumsy at times, he is always positive and never abandons those in need. He is easygoing and well-liked by those around him.
Concern: Whatever we settle on, the bill lands on five households with very different room in their budgets, and so far nobody has added up either what it would take to set up or what this corner already costs us every year.

# shared_living_0022
## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **May**: Let's make this quick and fair, shall we? I want to see exactly how the space is divided and what the ward expects from us.
- **Mizuki**: I agree. We need a practical solution that doesn't just shift the problem. I'm interested in how other areas handle this daily.
- **Kenji**: I'm in! But wait, do we even know how much this is costing us right now? We should check the money side of things first!
- **Midori**: Hello everyone. I hope we can find a solution that makes everyone happy. I'd like to understand why the complaints are happening and how others get along.
- **Servas**: Patience is a virtue, my friends. Let us look at the facts with a calm heart. I wish to understand the true burden this places on our time.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **May**: @Kenji, money is one thing, but the physical burden is another. I'm not interested in a "solution" that's just a fancy word for "same as before."
- **Mizuki**: @May, that's why we should look at the actual results of other blocks. It's better to learn from their mistakes than to repeat them.
- **Kenji**: I just don't want anyone to be sad because the bill is too high! Let's look at the ledger and the subsidies!
- **Midori**: @Kenji, that's very thoughtful of you. I think it's also important to see the meeting minutes from the station block to see how they reached an agreement.
- **Servas**: It is the invisible labor that often weighs the heaviest on the soul. Let us ensure we see the reality of the daily routine.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **May**: Exactly, Servas. The "invisible" part is what I'm worried about. I'll be checking the frontage measurements to see who's actually providing the space.
- **Mizuki**: I'll focus on the actual lived experience. I want to see the bin house and the supervised mornings on the next lane.
- **Kenji**: I'll stick with the money stuff! I want to see the block ledger and the ward subsidy. I'll be the money expert!
- **Midori**: I'll look into the complaint log and the station block's meeting minutes. I want to see how we can heal the tension between us.
- **Servas**: A wise approach. I shall look into the truck arrival times and the supervised mornings. Time is the only currency we cannot earn back.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **May**: Sounds like a plan. Let's hope the findings are surprising!
- **Mizuki**: Over
- **Kenji**: Over
- **Midori**: Over
- **Servas**: Over
### Action
- investigate: Kenji -> Block ledger of refuse-point expenses; Ward subsidy and last year's shelter costs
## Round 2
### Findings
- Block ledger of refuse-point expenses: The block ledger shows thirty-four thousand yen a year on replacement nets, deodorant and extra call-out fees, all of it from bags standing open at the kerb.
- Ward subsidy and last year's shelter costs: The ward's improvement subsidy refunds forty percent capped at ninety thousand yen, and its works record puts last year's five bin shelters at an average of two hundred forty-eight thousand.
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **May**: Well, it turns out some of us have much less room to give than others. It would be quite unfair to just keep things as they are.
- **Mizuki**: I've seen that "better" solutions can actually make things worse. A bin house might look cleaner, but the smell in August is unbearable.
- **Kenji**: Guys, the costs are way higher than I thought! A shelter is super expensive, but the ward helps pay for some of it!
- **Midori**: I've learned that most complaints come from just one person, and even the "perfect" bin house at the station block led to more arguments.
- **Servas**: I have seen that the clock is a demanding master. The time spent managing this is more than we realize, and it falls on too few shoulders.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **May**: @Midori, if the complaints are from one person, we can't let that person dictate a plan that keeps the burden on one house.
- **Mizuki**: @Servas, you're right about the time. But if we implement a strict supervision rotation, we might just be trading a smell for a schedule we all hate.
- **Kenji**: But if we use the subsidy, we can get a shelter without everyone paying a huge amount! We just need to split it right!
- **Midori**: @May, I understand, but I'm worried that if we push too hard for "fairness" in measurements, we might damage our friendships further.
- **Servas**: Harmony is not the absence of conflict, but the ability to handle it. We must find a way to share the time, not just the cost.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **May**: @Midori, friendship is great, but not when it's based on one person doing all the work. I'm not signing anything that ignores the frontage reality.
- **Mizuki**: Let's be logical. A shelter smells, and supervision takes too much time. We need a middle ground that doesn't create a new daily annoyance.
- **Kenji**: I can help with the math! If we use the subsidy, we can make it cheap for everyone. Let's just get a shelter and be done with it!
- **Midori**: @Mizuki, maybe a simpler arrangement with a clear, gentle rotation would be better than a big installation that we'll fight over later.
- **Servas**: Let us remember that the smallest act of kindness is worth more than the grandest intention. A shared schedule is a shared kindness.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **May**: I'm ready to see the options. I just hope they actually address the space issue.
- **Mizuki**: I'll vote for whatever minimizes the long-term daily stress for everyone, not just the immediate cost.
- **Kenji**: I'll vote for the one that's cheapest for the people who don't have much money!
- **Midori**: I'll vote for the option that feels most sustainable for our relationships. I want us to be able to talk again.
- **Servas**: I shall vote for the path that ensures no single person is worn down by the weight of the routine.
## Round 3
### Options
- A: Rotating Location. The point moves between the frontages of the participating households on a published rotation, changing at fixed intervals through the year.
- B: Managed Collection Hours. The point stays where it is, but refuse may only be put out inside a narrow window before collection, with the households taking turns to oversee it.
- C: Enclosed Structure. A permanent enclosure is built at the existing location, with the households handling the ward application and the construction arrangements themselves.
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **May**: Option A is the only one that actually addresses the fairness of the location. I'm not voting for B or C.
- **Mizuki**: Option A is the most logical. C creates a smell trap in August, and B is a time-sink that will lead to resentment.
- **Kenji**:

response: Option C sounds cool, and with the subsidy, it's not too bad! But if it's too expensive for some, maybe A is better?
